newsitem.title: UK: Murdered teacher focus for moral drive in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Murdered teacher focus for moral drive in Britain.

text.p: The widow of a headmaster knifed to death at the gates of his school has launched a campaign to change Britain's "moral climate", and politicians -- mindful of an election due by May at the latest -- are rushing to back her.

In a full-page article in Monday's Times, Frances Lawrence outlined her "manifesto for the nation" -- a call for a nationwide movement to banish violence, encourage children to learn civic values and promote the family.

Prime Minister John Major, Labour Party leader Tony Blair and Paddy Ashdown, leader of the minority Liberal Democrats, have all endorsed the crusade, and on Monday a government spokesman said: "Obviously Mrs Lawrence has struck a chord."

But as Lawrence launched her campaign to "rally the majority who have been silent for too long", the leaders of Britain's Roman Catholic church issued their own document on the need for a fair society, provoking a political row.

In a 13,000-word document, entitled The Common Good, the church leaders said employers should pay a just wage, warned that workers should not be treated as commodities and attacked the unacceptable gap that has grown between rich and poor.

Although the document, designed to guide Britain's five million Catholics in the run-up to the election, does not single out any political party, the media has interpreted it as a clear and blistering attack on the ruling Conservatives.
It offered support for a national minimum wage -- a declared Labour policy -- and criticism of social change which took place during 17 years of unbroken Conservative rule.
Major's office shrugged off the report. A spokesman said the prime minister had not seen a copy.

But the combination of Lawrence's call and the Catholic Church report -- given added weight on Monday by reports the Anglican and other churches were considering endorsing it -- has put the focus firmly on morals in the run-up to the election.
Philip Lawrence, 48, was killed in December as he tried to stop a gang attack a pupil at his London school. A 16-year-old boy was given a life sentence last Thursday for the killing.

The verdict came a day after the government announced a ban on most handguns in the wake of another school killing -- the massacre of 16 children and their teacher by crazed gunman Thomas Hamilton in the Scottish town of Dunblane in March.

The two killings, and recent trials like those of Fred and Rosemary West, who sexually tormented, killed and dismembered their young victims, and of the two 10-year-olds who killed two-year-old James Bulger in 1993, have prompted commentators to complain that the fabric of society is breaking down.

Blame for the collapse in values has been laid at the door of everything from violent videos, to the break-up of the family, the creation of an unemployed underclass and the collapse in esteem for institutions like the Royal Family.
